clinicalScope: Microcytic anaemia in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals, with emphasis on iron‑deficiency, thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease and sideroblastic anaemia
title: Microcytic Anaemia
subject: Medicine
summary: Microcytic anaemia is defined by a reduced mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and a low haemoglobin concentration. In low‑resource East African settings the most common causes are iron‑deficiency, thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease and, less frequently, sideroblastic anaemia.

sections.p: Microcytic anaemia is present when the MCV is below age‑adjusted cut‑offs and the haemoglobin is below normal for age and sex.
b: Children <6 months: MCV <70 fL
Children 6 months–2 years: MCV <75 fL
Children 2–6 years: MCV <77 fL
Children 6–12 years: MCV <80 fL
Children >12 years and adults: MCV <80 fL
Hb below WHO cut‑offs (e.g., <11 g/dL in children 6–59 months, <12 g/dL in non‑pregnant women, <13 g/dL in men)

sections.p: Severity guides urgency of treatment and need for transfusion.
b: Mild: Hb 10–11 g/dL (adults) or age‑appropriate mild drop
Moderate: Hb 7–9.9 g/dL
Severe: Hb <7 g/dL or symptomatic (tachycardia, hypotension, chest pain)
Very severe (life‑threatening): Hb <5 g/dL or signs of cardiac failure

sections.p: Identify the most probable aetiology based on epidemiology, diet, chronic disease and family history.
b: Iron‑deficiency anaemia – poor dietary iron, chronic intestinal blood loss, hookworm infection, heavy menstrual bleeding
Thalassaemia trait – family history, ethnic background (East African, Mediterranean, South Asian), very low MCV with normal Hb
Anaemia of chronic disease – HIV, tuberculosis, chronic kidney disease, rheumatic heart disease
Sideroblastic anaemia – alcohol excess, lead exposure, isoniazid, congenital X‑linked forms
Rare causes – congenital haemoglobinopathies (e.g., HbE), copper deficiency

sections.p: Symptoms reflect reduced oxygen‑carrying capacity and, occasionally, the underlying disease.
b: Fatigue, weakness, pallor, reduced exercise tolerance
Pica, restless legs, brittle nails (iron deficiency)
Mild jaundice or splenomegaly (thalassaemia trait)
Weight loss, night sweats, cough (TB or HIV‑related disease)
Abdominal pain, neuropathy (lead‑related sideroblastic anaemia)

sections.p: Select tests that answer the key diagnostic questions; note alternatives when resources are limited.

t.a: Full blood count with red‑cell indices
t.b: Confirms microcytosis and quantifies anaemia; low MCV and low MCH support microcytic aetiology
Answers: Is iron stores depleted? Low ferritin (<30 µg/L) confirms iron‑deficiency; normal/high ferritin suggests other causes
Answers: Is iron utilisation low? Saturation <15 % supports iron‑deficiency; >20 % points away from it
Answers: What is red‑cell morphology? Hypochromic microcytes suggest iron‑deficiency; target cells and basophilic stippling suggest thalassaemia or sideroblastic anaemia
Answers: Is marrow response adequate? Low retic (<1 %) in iron‑deficiency; normal/high in haemolysis
Answers: Is there inflammation? Elevated values support anaemia of chronic disease

t.a: Stool occult blood (if adult) or stool microscopy for ova
t.b: Answers: Is there gastrointestinal blood loss or helminth infection? Positive results guide treatment
Answers: Is a haemoglobinopathy present? Detects HbA2 elevation in β‑thalassaemia trait

sections.p: Recognise features that demand urgent intervention.
b: Severe Hb <7 g/dL with cardiovascular compromise
Rapid fall in Hb (>2 g/dL in 48 h)
Signs of heart failure (pulmonary oedema, peripheral oedema)
Persistent tachycardia >120 bpm at rest
Neurological symptoms in lead‑related sideroblastic anaemia

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then correct the anaemia.
b: Iron‑deficiency – oral ferrous salts (e.g., ferrous sulfate) for 3–6 months; give with vitamin C; monitor for GI side‑effects
Parenteral iron – consider if oral iron not tolerated, malabsorption, or rapid correction needed (e.g., late pregnancy, severe anaemia)
Thalassaemia trait – no specific therapy; counsel on genetics; avoid unnecessary iron
Anaemia of chronic disease – optimise control of HIV, TB, CKD; erythropoiesis‑stimulating agents only in selected CKD patients
Blood transfusion – reserve for severe or symptomatic anaemia; use packed RBCs, monitor for overload
Re‑check Hb and MCV 4–6 weeks after starting iron; expect Hb rise ≥1 g/dL if iron‑deficiency
For anaemia of chronic disease – monitor Hb together with disease activity; improvement follows disease control
Educate on iron‑rich diet (meat, beans, fortified cereals) and deworming every 6 months in endemic areas
Screen family members for thalassaemia trait if index case identified
Avoid routine iron supplementation in thalassaemia trait or anaemia of chronic disease

sections.p: Conditions that may mimic microcytic anaemia but have distinct features.
b: Macrocytic anaemia with laboratory error – MCV is genuinely high; repeat sample if discrepancy suspected
Hemolytic anaemia – typically normocytic or macrocytic with high retic count and elevated LDH
Anemia of acute blood loss – normocytic initially, becomes microcytic only after iron stores are exhausted

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Ferritin is an acute‑phase reactant; inflammation can raise ferritin masking iron‑deficiency – combine with CRP/ESR
Peripheral smear may show microcytosis from thalassaemia trait; RDW is often normal, unlike iron‑deficiency where RDW is raised
Transferrin saturation can be low in anaemia of chronic disease; interpret with ferritin and inflammatory markers

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of cardiac failure (dyspnoea, chest pain, peripheral oedema)

faq.q: Why is iron deficiency still common despite fortification programmes?
faq.a: Poor dietary intake, chronic intestinal parasites and limited access to fortified foods keep iron stores low in many low‑resource settings.

faq.q: Can a normal ferritin rule out iron deficiency?
faq.a: No; in the presence of infection or inflammation ferritin may be normal or high despite depleted iron stores.

faq.q: When is a blood transfusion indicated for microcytic anaemia?
faq.a: When Hb is <7 g/dL or the patient is symptomatic with cardiovascular compromise, after other causes have been addressed.

exam: A 9‑year‑old girl from a rural Kenyan clinic has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, and a stool exam positive for hookworm. What is the next step? — Start oral iron therapy and give albendazole; arrange follow‑up Hb in 4 weeks.
A patient with known β‑thalassaemia trait has Hb 11 g/dL, MCV 65 fL, normal ferritin. Should you give iron? — No; iron would not improve Hb and may cause overload.

In a malaria‑endemic area, a child with Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, and a negative malaria smear is found to have low ferritin. What is the priority treatment? — Oral iron supplementation; malaria treatment only if smear becomes positive.

A pregnant woman in her third trimester has Hb 6.5 g/dL, MCV 78 fL, and cannot tolerate oral iron due to vomiting. What is appropriate? — Consider parenteral iron (e.g., iron sucrose) after ruling out infection.

A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with anaemia, MCV 75 fL, basophilic stippling, and a history of lead‑based paint exposure. What specific therapy should be added? — Pyridoxine trial and removal of lead exposure; chelation if blood lead >45 µg/dL.
How does RDW help differentiate iron‑deficiency from thalassaemia trait? — RDW is markedly increased in iron‑deficiency but usually normal in thalassaemia trait.
What is the most important monitoring parameter after starting oral iron in a child? — Rise in haemoglobin of at least 1 g/dL after 4 weeks, together with improvement in symptoms.
